Background Obesity is a serious disease that is associated with an increased risk of diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, stroke, and cancer, among other diseases. The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates a 20% obesity rate in the 50 states, with 12 states having rates of over 30%. Currently, the body mass index (BMI) is most commonly used to determine adiposity. However, BMI presents as an inaccurate obesity classification method that underestimates the epidemic and contributes to failed treatment. In this study, we examine the effectiveness of precise biomarkers and duel-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) to help diagnose and treat obesity. Methodology/Principal Findings A cross-sectional study of adults with BMI, DXA, fasting leptin and insulin results were measured from 1998–2009. Of the participants, 63% were females, 37% were males, 75% white, with a mean age = 51.4 (SD = 14.2). Mean BMI was 27.3 (SD = 5.9) and mean percent body fat was 31.3% (SD = 9.3). BMI characterized 26% of the subjects as obese, while DXA indicated that 64% of them were obese. 39% of the subjects were classified as non-obese by BMI, but were found to be obese by DXA. BMI misclassified 25% men and 48% women. Meanwhile, a strong relationship was demonstrated between increased leptin and increased body fat. Conclusions/Significance Our results demonstrate the prevalence of false-negative BMIs, increased misclassifications in women of advancing age, and the reliability of gender-specific revised BMI cutoffs. BMI underestimates obesity prevalence, especially in women with high leptin levels (>30 ng/mL). Clinicians can use leptin-revised levels to enhance the accuracy of BMI estimates of percentage body fat when DXA is unavailable. Introduction Global trends of increasing obesity threaten public health and contribute to the burden of disease as much as smoking does [1] , [2] . Obesity is associated with increased risk of diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, stroke, cancer, dyslipidemia, liver and gallbladder disease, sleep apnea and respiratory problems, osteoarthritis, abnormal menses and infertility [3] . Adiposity in mid-life strongly relates to reduced probability of healthy long term survival in women [4] . Obesity has become a priority of national, state and local public health efforts and in the care of individual patients. Thus, clinical detection of obese individuals has commensurately reached critical importance. With the increasing importance of obesity detection, it is useful to reevaluate how body fat is determined. For adults, the body mass index (BMI) is commonly used. Its popularity stems in part from its convenience, safety, and minimal cost, and its use is widespread, despite not being able to distinguish lean body mass from fat mass [5] . The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) explain: “For adults, overweight and obesity ranges are determined by using weight and height to calculate a number called the “body mass index” (BMI). BMI is used because, for most people, it correlates with their amount of body fat” [6] . However, the BMI is actually an indirect surrogate measurement considered imprecise [7] , [8] . Recent estimates from NHANES, a nationally representative health examination survey, project that approximately 34% of adult Americans are overweight (defined as a BMI between 25–30 kg/m 2 ) and an additional 34% are obese (BMI >30 kg/m 2 ) [9] . In contrast, the CDC estimates rates of obesity over 20% in all 50 states with estimated rates over 30% in 12 states [ http://www.cdc.gov/obesity ]. These estimates are fundamental to US policy addressing the epidemic of obesity and are central to designing interventions aimed at curbing its growth, yet they may be flawed because they are based on the BMI. The outdated BMI formula [BMI = weight in pounds/(height in inches) 2 ×703], developed nearly 200 years ago by Quetelet, is not a measurement of adiposity, but merely an imprecise mathematical estimate [7] , [8] , [10] – [14] . Defining obesity based on percent body fat, as with BMI, also has arbitrary cut-points. In 1995, the World Health Organization (WHO) defined obesity based on a percent body fat ≥25% for men and ≥35% for women [15] , while the most recent 2009 guidelines from the American Society of Bariatric Physicians (ASBP), an American Medical Association (AMA) specialty board, used percent body fat ≥25% for men and ≥30% for women. The ASBP percent body fat guidelines identify individuals that are suitable candidates for treatment for obesity with anorectic agents. Most studies comparing BMI with more accurate measures of adiposity used cutoffs of body fat >25% for men and >30% for women [16] . BMI ignores several important factors affecting adiposity. Greater loss of muscle mass leading to sarcopenic obesity in women occurs increasingly with age. BMI does not acknowledge this factor, exacerbating misclassifications [17] , [18] . Furthermore, men's BMI also does not consider the inverse relationship between muscular strength and mortality [19] . It fails to take into account that men lose less muscle with age than women. Statistical models have been created to explain variance in leptin with relation to insulin, gender, and BMI, but lack a variable of direct adiposity measurement such as DXA [20] . A fully equipped duel-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) provides simultaneous measurements of muscle, bone mass and body adiposity. The ASBP uses both BMI and DXA as criteria for interventions. Studies comparing DXA-derived percent body fat rates of obesity to BMI have, to date, focused mainly on women [12] , [21] or imputed data on percent body fat for a substantial proportion of subjects [14] . We sought to characterize the degree of misclassification of obesity based on BMI using percent body fat from DXA in a large, unselected population, and to use the more accurate DXA derived measure to identify the optimal cut-points for defining obesity using BMI. Reclassifying obesity cut points is worth considering, as there is a population of individuals with a normal BMI who nonetheless have increased adiposity as determined by more sensitive methods; these are the so-called ‘normal weight obese.’ These individuals may have increased risk for medical comorbidities such as hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, hypertension, and diabetes [7] . Furthermore, in the intermediate ranges, BMI is not a good discriminator of cardiovascular risk; use of adiposity measures rather than BMI may be a better predictor, but have recently failed [22] – [25] . Therefore, there is a need to reclassify the obesity epidemic, identify clinically useful biomarkers, and clarify what the medical and scientific communities are measuring with BMI. Although DXA is a direct measurement of fat and a better measure of adiposity than BMI, it is not a disease correlate. The attempts to find disease correlates to explain disparities between BMI and direct fat measurements have included leptin, insulin, ghrelin, and adiponectin [26] . Leptin, a 16 kDa peptide secreted primarily by adipocytes, regulates the body's energy balance by acting as a negative feedback adiposity signal, decreasing food intake and increasing energy expenditure. In individuals with leptin insensitive receptors, neither transport nor action is possible, and leptin levels rise [27] . Increased leptin is associated with the inflammatory process and possibly the entire increased morbidity of obesity [28] , [29] . Individuals with leptin insensitivity and high levels of leptin have parallel comorbidities to normal weight obesity such as chronic inflammation, type II diabetes, hypertension, and myocardial injury [ http://www.asbp.org/siterun_data/about_asbp/position_statements/doc7270523281295654373.html ]. Therefore, it was appropriate to investigate whether leptin levels could correct for the disparity between DXA and BMI and be used to create a more accurate measure of obesity.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Obesity classification and adiposity measurement relative to DXA-derived percent body fat
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: BMI misclassified 39% of subjects as non-obese who were obese by DXA. Specifically, 25% of men and 48% of women were misclassified. Overall, BMI characterized 26% of subjects as obese compared to 64% by DXA, significantly underestimating adiposity and obesity prevalence.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Body fat correlation, obesity management, and high-risk obesity prediction
core_effect_and_quantification.direction_of_change: Increased (with increased body fat); lowering (for weight control)
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: A strong positive relationship exists between increased leptin levels and increased body fat. Hyperleptinemia, particularly in women (91% of high leptin patients), is more significant than BMI in predicting high-risk obesity. Leptin levels above 30 ng/mL are associated with BMI underestimation of obesity prevalence in women. Lowering elevated leptin levels has significant impacts on long-term weight control.
No clear relationship was demonstrated between insulin levels and percent body fat.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Obesity classification and correlation with comorbidities
core_effect_and_quantification.direction_of_change: Increased (with obesity); gold standard for measurement
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: DXA-derived percent body fat is considered the gold standard for defining obesity and correlates better than BMI with obesity co-morbidities.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Obesity and adiposity regulation, classification, and weight management
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Leptin, a peptide secreted by adipocytes, regulates energy balance by decreasing food intake and increasing energy expenditure. Leptin insensitive receptors lead to increased leptin levels, correlating with inflammatory processes and increased obesity morbidity. BMI significantly underestimates obesity prevalence due to its inability to distinguish fat from lean mass, particularly affecting women (especially with advancing age and sarcopenic obesity) and potentially missing the inverse relationship between muscle strength and mortality in men. Hyperleptinemia, prevalent in women, contributes to inaccurate BMI-based obesity diagnoses and impacts long-term weight control. While leptin levels strongly correlate with percent body fat and improve BMI's precision (especially in women), insulin levels do not show a clear relationship with body fat. Direct adiposity measurements like DXA provide a more comprehensive assessment of body composition and disease risk.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: BMI significantly underestimates adiposity and obesity prevalence, with misclassification rates higher in women (48%) than men (25%), increasing further in women of advancing age. Current NIH BMI criteria (≥30) show low sensitivity, particularly for women with high leptin levels (>30 ng/mL). Optimized, gender-specific BMI cut-points (e.g., >24 for females, >28 for males) are proposed to improve diagnostic sensitivity; for instance, female BMI sensitivity increased from 35% (at BMI 30) to 79% (at BMI 24) with a minor specificity decrease. Leptin levels are particularly useful for BMI adjustment in women when BMI is ≤25.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: BMI lacks specificity as it cannot distinguish lean body mass from fat mass and fails to account for age-related muscle loss (sarcopenic obesity) in women or muscle strength in men, leading to significant misclassifications. Its association with percent body fat is modulated by sex and age, with misclassification more prevalent in women (48%) than men (25%), and increasing with age in women (e.g., 59% for ages 70+). In contrast, DXA provides precise measurements of muscle, bone mass, and body adiposity. Leptin levels enhance BMI's precision, and adiposity along with hyperleptinemia are stronger predictors of high-risk obesity than BMI, with leptin showing the strongest correlation with obesity rates among biomarkers.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Adults (≥18 years old), including a focus on women (especially of advancing age, postmenopausal, and those with high leptin levels), men, older individuals, 'normal weight obese' patients, and the broader American population.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Obesity is associated with numerous comorbidities including diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, stroke, cancer, dyslipidemia, liver/gallbladder disease, sleep apnea, respiratory problems, osteoarthritis, abnormal menses, and infertility. Mid-life adiposity reduces healthy long-term survival in women. Misclassification by current BMI criteria leads to false-negative diagnoses, hindering prevention and management of these conditions. 'Normal weight obese' individuals and those with leptin insensitivity/high leptin levels are at increased risk for hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, chronic inflammation, type II diabetes, hypertension, and myocardial injury. Improved diagnostic accuracy through gender-specific BMI cut-points and leptin incorporation can lead to better obesity management, enhanced long-term weight control, reduced risk of impaired gait, disability, falls, and fractures in women, and more effective prediction and prevention of these medical comorbidities.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Diagnostic utility for more accurate obesity assessment (using DXA, leptin-revised levels, and gender-specific BMI cutoffs); adverse risk associated with BMI misclassification leading to underestimated obesity prevalence, failed treatment, and unaddressed comorbidities like hyperleptinemia, increased adiposity, and sarcopenia; and protective benefits derived from improved long-term weight control and more precise adiposity measurement for intervention.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: BMI is consistently assessed as an unreliable, inaccurate, and flawed method for obesity classification. It significantly underestimates true obesity prevalence, particularly in women and with advancing age, due to its inability to distinguish fat mass from lean mass. DXA-derived percent body fat is considered highly reliable and the 'gold standard' for adiposity measurement. Leptin levels are deemed a reliable and useful tool for enhancing the precision of BMI estimates, especially in women, showing a stronger correlation with obesity rates than other biomarkers, though further studies are recommended for its full integration. Insulin levels were found to be unreliably related to percent body fat.
recommended_alternatives: Duel-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) as the gold standard for adiposity assessment
Leptin measurements (especially leptin-revised levels or levels >30 ng/mL) as an adjunct to BMI for improved precision, particularly in women
Adoption of new, gender-specific BMI cut-points (e.g., >24 kg/m² for females, >28 kg/m² for males) to enhance diagnostic sensitivity
Further studies on leptin measurements to fully integrate its potential as a biomarker
